summary: This document defines the next-hop-aliases parameter for the HTTP Proxy-Status field. It carries the list of aliases and canonical names that an intermediary saw during DNS resolution when connecting to the next hop.

plainLanguage.summary: A delivery helper can write a note on the receipt of the other names a place went by when they looked up its address. This helps debug trouble.

questions: how does a proxy report cname chains
subtitle: A Proxy-Status parameter that lets a proxy report the full chain of DNS alias names it saw on the way to the next hop.

tldr.problem: The existing next-hop parameter in Proxy-Status holds only one hostname, address or alias, so a client cannot learn the chain of CNAME names a proxy met while resolving the next hop.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9532 defines a next-hop-aliases parameter whose value is a String holding a comma-separated list of the alias and canonical names received in DNS CNAME records.
tldr.outcome: Clients of a proxy can see when a harmless-looking hostname is a cloak for a tracker or malicious host, but the list is only a hint and is only as trustworthy as the proxy and its resolvers.

today: RFC 9532 is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC in the metadata. It extends the Proxy-Status field defined in RFC 9209.

sections.title: Why Report Alias Names
sections.content:
The Proxy-Status HTTP response field lets an intermediary tell clients how it handled a request. Its next-hop parameter can carry a hostname, an IP address or an alias of the next hop, but only one of them. It cannot describe a whole chain of aliases found during DNS resolution.

That chain matters most to clients of forward proxies, where the client asks the proxy to connect to a specific target using the CONNECT method or UDP proxying. CNAME records can be used to cloak hosts that track users or do malicious things behind more innocent-looking names. Web browsers use the chain of DNS names to shape behavior such as cookie policies or blocking of malicious hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a place has a nickname that hides its real name. The receipt only had room for one name, so you could not see the nicknames. Now there is room for all of them.

sections.title: The next-hop-aliases Parameter
sections.content:
The value of next-hop-aliases is a String (as defined for HTTP structured fields) containing one or more DNS names in a comma-separated list. The list holds every alias name and canonical name received in CNAME records while resolving the next hop's hostname, and it MAY also include the original requested hostname itself.

The names ought to appear in the order they were received in DNS. The first name is the value of the CNAME record for the original hostname, and the last name is the one that finally resolved to one or more addresses.

The parameter can be sent without next-hop. A proxy MAY send the empty string as the value to say that no CNAME records were met. The parameter applies only when DNS was used to resolve the next hop's name, so clients need to handle its absence gracefully.

A proxy acting as a reverse proxy can put the next hop's own name first in the list. This helps when next-hop carries only an IP address and the client would otherwise not know the name.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper writes the names in the order the lookup found them, like a trail of clues, and writes nothing but an empty note if there were no nicknames.

sections.title: Encoding Special Characters
sections.content:
DNS names usually contain only letters, digits and hyphens, but they may contain any character, including a comma. To keep a comma inside a name from breaking the list, every character that is not a URI unreserved character MUST be percent-encoded.

A period inside a label, as opposed to a separator between labels, MUST first be escaped as \.. Because the backslash is then percent-encoded, dot\.label.example.com becomes dot%5C.label.example.com, and on parsing, dot%5C.label MUST be treated as a single label. A backslash in a label MUST be escaped as \\ and then percent-encoded. Other uses of the backslash MUST NOT appear after percent-decoding.
sections.plainLanguage: If a name has a comma in it, writing it plainly would look like two names. So the comma gets a secret code, like writing the word for it instead.

sections.title: Getting the Chain From the Resolver
sections.content:
To send the parameter, a proxy needs access to the chain of alias and canonical names from the CNAME records. The RFC warns that common resolution APIs such as getaddrinfo may not expose the full chain. Its AI_CANONNAME option returns only the last name, the canonical name, and not the aliases before it.

An implementation MAY therefore send incomplete information, for example only the canonical name, when it cannot see the whole chain.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tools only tell the helper the final name, not the nicknames along the way. The helper is allowed to write just what it knows.

sections.title: How Far to Trust the List
sections.content:
The parameter carries no DNSSEC information and does not imply that DNSSEC was used. The client can trust it only as far as it trusts the proxy. It is meant as a hint and SHOULD NOT be used to make security decisions about the identity of a resource reached through the proxy.

Inspecting CNAME chains can reveal cloaked trackers or malicious hosts, but a recursive or authoritative resolver that wants to hide cloaking could omit the CNAME records, and a malicious proxy could simply not report them. In general, clients can trust what is included or left out only to the degree that the proxy and its resolvers are trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is only as honest as the helper who wrote it. If the helper or the phone book hides a nickname, you will not see it.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The document registers next-hop-aliases in the HTTP Proxy-Status Parameters registry. The registered description is a string containing one or more DNS aliases or canonical names used to establish a proxied connection to the next hop.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note field gets written in the official list of allowed fields so everyone knows it exists.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE FROM RFC 9532: TWO CNAMES THEN AN ADDRESS

data.title: DNS records and the resulting field
data.code:
host.example.com.      CNAME   tracker.example.com.
tracker.example.com.   CNAME   service1.example.com.
service1.example.com.  AAAA    2001:db8::1

Proxy-Status: proxy.example.net; next-hop="2001:db8::1";
    next-hop-aliases="tracker.example.com,service1.example.com"
